proposals.relationship: Wolfe adapts Mauss’s total social phenomenon to analyse anthropology as a total discursive practice participating in colonial settlement.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1999 introduction 3 explicitly identifies the adaptation, while note 6 quotes Mauss 1925 [1970]:1 on simultaneously religious, legal, moral, economic, aesthetic and morphological institutions. Wolfe treats anthropological debates as primary data rather than adjudicating their claims about Indigenous life. This is a particular methodological resource, not equivalence between the two complete projects or a newly read Mauss original; bracketed 1970 does not become first publication.
primary_locators: 1999 Cassell edition, Introduction, printed 3 and note 6

proposals.relationship: Wolfe uses Spivak’s distinction between exposing mechanisms and making individuals speak to explain his refusal of ethnographic ventriloquism.
proposals.evidence_note: Own introduction 4 invokes Spivak 1988:288 while distinguishing the analysis of anthropological constructions from an attempt to recuperate an allegedly pristine Indigenous voice behind them. Political and empirical methodological limits converge in his argument. This records his explicit use of a particular distinction, not proof he adopted all of Spivak’s work, a claim Indigenous people had no voice, or a newly read Spivak original; the cited original title is not guessed.
primary_locators: 1999 Cassell edition, Introduction, printed 4, paragraph beginning “Hence there are both political and methodological reasons”

proposals.relationship: Chakrabarty supervised and commented on the entire doctoral draft from which substantial portions of Wolfe’s first book developed.
proposals.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments vii distinguish three successive supervisors, Maurice Bloch, Greg Dening and finally Chakrabarty; the last read and commented on the whole draft. This is specific critical scholarly input to the thesis, not a claim he alone formed Wolfe or read the final 1999 book. Wolfe explicitly separates the later rewritten book and the whole-book readings by Phillip Darby and Michele Grossman. No particular adopted revision or common theoretical doctrine is invented.
primary_locators: 1999 Cassell edition, Acknowledgements, printed vii, second paragraph; subsequent paragraphs distinguish rewritten book
